title: Magnetic resonance imaging characteristics of glioblastoma of the optic pathway during adulthood
case_prompt: A 46-year-old man presented with a 6-week history of progressive visual loss. He first noticed gradual visual decline in his left eye, progressing to complete blindness, and partial vision loss in his right eye. He denied headaches, jaw claudication, or pain with eye movement. On examination, there was reduced pupillary reactivity to light in the left eye and discoloration of the right eye; no other neurologic deficits were present. Brain MRI with intravenous contrast revealed a diffuse lesion involving the left optic nerve and optic chiasm, extending along the optic tract, optic radiation, and pituitary stalk. The lesion demonstrated hyperintensity on T2-weighted and FLAIR sequences, heterogeneous enhancement on postcontrast T1-weighted images, and an apparent diffusion coefficient of 1.049 × 10−3 mm2/s. These findings were interpreted as consistent with a high-grade optic pathway glioma (modified Dodge grade 3).
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. NAION was considered given the optic neuropathy but was atypical due to the patient’s younger age and subacute progression — “Differential diagnoses encompass NAION, which usually occurs in patients aged >50 years and presents with sudden visual loss either ipsilaterally or bilaterally.”  
2. Optic neuritis was considered in a younger patient with unilateral vision loss but typically shows rapid corticosteroid responsiveness — “Another candidate is optic nerve inflammation occurring on one side in patients aged <50 years and rapidly responding to corticosteroid therapy.”  
3. Retinal vein occlusion was considered due to overlapping ophthalmic features but imaging showed an infiltrative mass rather than vascular occlusion — “Retinal vein occlusion and temporal arteritis should also be considered as differential diagnoses owing to some overlapping features.”  
4. Temporal arteritis was considered for subacute vision loss but was less likely given the absence of headache, jaw claudication, or temporal pain — “He denied any headache, intermittent jaw pain, or temporal region pain relating to eyeball movement.”  
5. Optic nerve sheath meningioma was considered for optic nerve involvement but typically demonstrates a tram-track sign on imaging, which was absent — “Optic nerve sheath meningioma commonly arises surrounding cranial nerve II, with tram track signs of meningioma.”  
6. Sellar and suprasellar neoplasms were considered for chiasmal lesions but usually do not enhance the optic nerve itself — “Sellar and suprasellar neoplasms typically occur at the optic chiasm but show no optic nerve enhancement.”  
7. Multiple sclerosis and other short-segment demyelinating lesions were considered but would not present as a diffuse infiltrative mass — “Nontumoral lesions encompass infectious and noninfectious inflammation of cranial nerve II, including multiple sclerosis (ipsilateral and short segment).”  
8. Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorders and anti-MOG encephalomyelitis were considered for bilateral long-segment optic involvement but typically involve the spinal cord and respond to steroids — “Nontumoral lesions encompass infectious and noninfectious inflammation of cranial nerve II, including multiple sclerosis (ipsilateral and short segment), neuromyelitis optica, and anti-MOG encephalomyelitis (bilateral, long segment, and spinal involvement).”  
9. Other tumoral or granulomatous processes (e.g., lymphoma, metastasis, infectious inflammation) were considered but require histopathology for differentiation — “Both nerve and nerve sheath involvements include high- and low-grade gliomas, secondary perineuronal inflammation due to infection, granulomatous inflammation, lymphoma, and metastasis.”
